summary: Defines the SIP REFER method, which asks the receiver to contact a resource named in the request, and lets the sender be told how that attempt turned out. This underlies features such as call transfer. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: You ask a receptionist to call someone for you, and she tells you whether they picked up. This memo lets one phone call software ask another to contact somebody, and report back what happened. It is how calls get transferred.

questions: how does sip call transfer work
what does 202 accepted mean for sip refer
subtitle: How one SIP endpoint can ask another to contact a third party, and then hear how it went.

tldr.problem: SIP had no clean way to tell an endpoint 'go contact this resource for me' and learn the result, which is what features such as call transfer need.
tldr.mechanism: The REFER method carries one Refer-To header with the target URI. The recipient asks for approval, contacts the target, and reports progress to the sender in NOTIFY requests that carry a message/sipfrag body, through an implicit subscription to the 'refer' event package.
tldr.outcome: REFER gives SIP a general 'refer to this resource' request with built-in status reporting, motivated by call transfer. The RFC warns that acting on arbitrary URIs and reporting detailed results both carry security risks.

facts.label: Notification rate
facts.value: No more than once per second

today: RFC 3515 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7647 and RFC 8217. Read those alongside this document.

sections.title: What REFER Does
sections.content:
This document defines the REFER method, a SIP extension that asks the recipient to contact a resource named in the request. It also defines the refer event package and the Refer-To request header field.

Its flagship use is call transfer. If Alice is in a call with Bob and decides Bob needs to talk to Carol, Alice's user agent sends a REFER to Bob's user agent with Carol's contact information. Assuming Bob has given permission, Bob's user agent tries to call Carol and then reports to Alice's user agent whether it reached her.

REFER is a SIP method as defined by RFC 3261, and unless stated otherwise it is sent and answered like a BYE. It may be sent outside a dialog created by an INVITE; REFER itself creates a dialog. A REFER also implicitly sets up a subscription to the refer event, using the event machinery of RFC 3265.
sections.plainLanguage: Alice asks Bob to call Carol, and Bob promises to tell Alice whether Carol answered. That is how a call gets handed over.

sections.title: The Refer-To Header
sections.content:
A REFER request MUST contain exactly one Refer-To header field value, which holds the URI to reference. The header also has the compact form r. It appears only in REFER requests and may be encrypted end to end. The target is not put in Contact, because Contact is part of the Route/Record-Route mechanism.

The target need not be a SIP address. The RFC's own examples include a SIP URI with a method=SUBSCRIBE parameter and an http: URL. A REFER may carry a body, but the RFC assigns it no meaning.

A recipient MUST answer 400 (Bad Request) if the request has zero or more than one Refer-To value.
sections.plainLanguage: Refer-To is the sticky note with the name and number of the person to call.

sections.title: Handling a REFER Request
sections.content:
A user agent that accepts a well-formed REFER SHOULD ask its user for approval, either interactively or through configured policy. If approval is granted, it MUST contact the resource in the Refer-To URI by the normal mechanism for that URI type. For a SIP INVITE URI, that means a new INVITE built by the usual rules. A user agent that cannot reach non-SIP URIs SHOULD NOT accept REFERs to them.

The recipient MAY answer 100 (Trying) or any suitable 4xx to 6xx. Otherwise it MUST return 202 Accepted before the REFER transaction expires. Once it accepts with a 2xx, it MUST create a subscription and send notifications about the outcome.

Proxies need no changes: a proxy treats a REFER like an OPTIONS request. A registrar unaware of REFER returns 501, and one that knows REFER SHOULD return 405.
sections.plainLanguage: Bob first checks that he is allowed to make the call, says 'okay, I will try', and then goes and does it.

sections.title: Reporting Results with NOTIFY
sections.content:
The sender learns the outcome through NOTIFY requests. Each one MUST have an Event: refer header and a body of type message/sipfrag that begins with a SIP response status line. The response class says how the referenced action is going. The refer package does not support state deltas, so every body is a full statement of status.

A minimal implementation can send a single NOTIFY with SIP/2.0 100 Trying while pending, SIP/2.0 200 OK on success, SIP/2.0 503 Service Unavailable on failure, or SIP/2.0 603 Declined if approval was later denied. This also works for non-SIP targets: a successful fetch of an HTTP URL can be reported as SIP/2.0 200 OK.

Creating a subscription always triggers an immediate NOTIFY, so the sender must be ready for one before the REFER transaction finishes. The subscription's duration is chosen by the accepting agent and sent in the first NOTIFY. The final NOTIFY MUST say the subscription is terminated with reason noresource. Notifications SHOULD NOT be sent more than once per second.

Only a REFER can create a subscription to the refer event; a SUBSCRIBE for a nonexistent one MUST be rejected with 403. If the sender unsubscribes early, that does not withdraw the referenced request, and the recipient SHOULD NOT send a CANCEL for that reason. When a second REFER is sent in the same dialog, NOTIFYs MUST include an id parameter in the Event header, carrying the CSeq number of the REFER they belong to.
sections.plainLanguage: Bob texts Alice 'trying', then 'got through' or 'could not reach them'. A short note is enough.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3261 apply, with extra attention to who may send REFERs and to what NOTIFY bodies reveal.

On authorization, a REFER can name a URI with any scheme, such as an HTTP URL. An agent that follows such URIs automatically risks being used to attack another host, especially one behind the same firewall. So the user must normally approve interactively, with the full URI shown. A display name alone is not enough, since nothing ties it to the URI. Policy-based acceptance may suit a properly authenticated REFER inside an existing dialog to a sip:, sips: or tel: URI.

On reporting, copying every response into NOTIFY bodies can leak information. In the RFC's examples, an attacker can use a helpful agent to learn that a person is online and her agent's IP address, or to learn a server's product name. The RFC advises returning only a carefully chosen subset, and the minimal status-line-only approach reveals the least.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not let a stranger talk you into calling a number without checking it, and do not tell them every detail of what you saw.

sections.title: Why It Looks This Way
sections.content:
The method was motivated by call transfer. It started as TRANSFER, was generalized to REFER, and improved on the BYE/Also idea from an expired draft by separating transfers from BYE processing. That makes failed transfers easier to recover from and clarifies state in the parties involved.

Early versions made the recipient wait until the referred action finished before sending its final response. That was infeasible given the transaction timeout rules for non-INVITE requests. A REFER must always get an immediate final response, which is why the result travels in NOTIFYs.
sections.plainLanguage: Waiting on the phone while Bob made the other call took too long, so he answers right away and reports later.

items.label: Declined
items.desc: Accepted first, but approval to follow the reference was then denied.
